claim: The segmentation gene network in insects can produce equivalent phenotypic outputs despite differences in upstream regulatory inputs between species.
source: The segmentation gene network in insects can produce equivalent phenotypic outputs despite differences in upstream regulatory inputs between species.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about insect segmentation networks, supported by the study's findings.

claim: Initiation and dynamics of gap gene expression differ markedly between M. abdita and Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Initiation and dynamics of gap gene expression differ markedly between M. abdita and Drosophila melanogaster
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative expression data presented throughout the manuscript comparing the two species.

claim: The output of the gap gene system converges to equivalent patterns at the end of the blastoderm stage between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: while the output of the system converges to equivalent patterns at the end of the blastoderm stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative expression data showing convergence at C14A-T8 stage.

claim: The qualitative structure of the gap gene network is conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Although the qualitative structure of the gap gene network is conserved, there are differences in the strength of regulatory interactions between species.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi knock-down experiments showing similar types of interactions in both species.

claim: There are differences in the strength of regulatory interactions between M. abdita and D. melanogaster gap gene networks.
source: Although the qualitative structure of the gap gene network is conserved, there are differences in the strength of regulatory interactions between species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of RNAi knock-down effects showing altered interaction strengths.

claim: Quantitative system drift provides a mechanistic explanation for the developmental hourglass model in the dipteran lineage.
source: It provides a mechanistic explanation for the developmental hourglass model in the dipteran lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early expression differs but converges later, consistent with the hourglass model.

claim: Quantitative system drift is likely to be a widespread mechanism for developmental evolution.
source: Quantitative system drift is likely to be a widespread mechanism for developmental evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings in this study and general principles of network evolution.

claim: The gap gene system in Drosophila melanogaster is one of the most thoroughly studied developmental gene regulatory networks.
source: The gap gene system in Drosophila melanogaster (family: Drosophilidae) is one of the most thoroughly studied developmental gene regulatory networks today.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous research on the D. melanogaster gap gene system.

claim: Mathematical models exist that faithfully reproduce gap gene expression dynamics in D. melanogaster.
source: a number of mathematical models exist that faithfully reproduce gap gene expression dynamics in this species
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to modeling studies.

claim: M. abdita belongs to the brachyceran infra-order Cyclorrhapha.
source: M. abdita belongs to the brachyceran infra-order Cyclorrhapha (marked in red)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1 phylogenetic tree.

claim: Only cyclorrhaphan flies have a bcd gene.
source: Only cyclorrhaphan flies have a bcd gene.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and shown in the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Posterior patterning is delayed in the moth midge Clogmia albipunctata compared to D. melanogaster.
source: Qualitative (Rohr et al., 1999; García-Solache et al., 2010; Jiménez-Guri et al., 2014) and quantitative (Crombach et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2014) studies of segmentation gene expression in the moth midge Clogmia albipunctata (family: Psychodidae) indicate that posterior patterning—especially the onset of posterior hb expression—is delayed
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on C. albipunctata.

claim: Maternal transcripts of bcd and hb can be detected in M. abdita.
source: Maternal transcripts of bcd and hb can be detected (Stauber et al., 1999, 2000; Lemke et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No maternal contribution to cad expression is present in M. abdita.
source: but no maternal contribution to cad expression is present in this species (Stauber et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Localised maternal bcd transcripts at the anterior pole extend further posterior in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Localised maternal bcd transcripts at the anterior pole extend further posterior, and bcd RNAi cuticle phenotypes affect more posterior segments than in D. melanogaster
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in this manuscript.

claim: bcd RNAi cuticle phenotypes affect more posterior segments in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Localised maternal bcd transcripts at the anterior pole extend further posterior, and bcd RNAi cuticle phenotypes affect more posterior segments than in D. melanogaster, indicating a broader role of Bcd in M. abdita
evidence: This is supported by citations and indicates functional differences.

claim: The zygotic anterior hb domain is severely depleted in M. abdita embryos treated with bcd RNAi.
source: The zygotic anterior hb domain is severely depleted in embryos treated with bcd RNAi, suggesting activation of hb by Bcd as in D. melanogaster
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study and suggests conserved regulatory interaction.

claim: Gap gene expression differs significantly between M. abdita and D. melanogaster during early to mid blastoderm stage.
source: Our comparison reveals that gap gene expression differs significantly between the two species during early to mid blastoderm stage but converges to equivalent patterns before the onset of gastrulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative expression data comparing the two species.

claim: The broader influence of Bcd in M. abdita causes gap domains to emerge at more posterior positions compared to D. melanogaster.
source: In particular, we find that the broader influence of Bcd in M. abdita causes gap domains to emerge at more posterior positions compared to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is inferred from bcd expression data and RNAi experiments.

claim: The absence of maternal Cad causes a delay in the onset of anterior shifts of posterior gap domains in M. abdita.
source: In addition, the absence of maternal Cad causes a delay in the onset of anterior shifts of posterior gap domains in M. abdita.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with D. melanogaster and cad germ-line clone experiments.

claim: The delay in posterior gap domain shifts in M. abdita is later compensated by stronger shifts compared to D. melanogaster.
source: This delay is later compensated by stronger shifts compared to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative boundary position data over time.

claim: Embryos were stained by single or double in situ hybridisation using an enzymatic (colorimetric) protocol.
source: wild-type or RNAi-treated embryos were stained by single or double in situ hybridisation using an enzymatic (colorimetric) protocol as described in Crombach et al. (2012a)
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Boundary positions are extracted by fitting clamped splines to domain boundaries in intensity profiles.
source: After the extraction of the intensity profile within this strip (magenta line in graph), we manually fit clamped splines to domain boundaries (black lines with mid- and end-points indicated by circles).
evidence: This describes the data extraction method shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain is stable in D. melanogaster.
source: In D. melanogaster, the posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain is stable, while this border shifts to the anterior in M. abdita
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B comparing boundary positions over time.

claim: The posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain shifts to the anterior in M. abdita.
source: In D. melanogaster, the posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain is stable, while this border shifts to the anterior in M. abdita
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with quantitative boundary position data.

claim: M. abdita has a stable posterior domain of anterior gt.
source: while this border shifts to the anterior in M. abdita, which has a stable posterior domain of anterior gt instead
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B comparing gt expression dynamics.

claim: Gap genes are initiated more posteriorly in M. abdita compared to D. melanogaster in the posterior region of the embryo.
source: Moreover, in the posterior region of the embryo, gap genes are initiated more posteriorly in M. abdita compared to D. melanogaster
evidence: This is demonstrated by boundary position data in Figure 3B.

claim: Patterning is delayed with posterior gap domains retracting from the pole at later stages in M. abdita.
source: and patterning is delayed with posterior gap domains retracting from the pole and shifting to the anterior at later stages in M. abdita
evidence: This is shown by temporal expression data in Figure 3B.

claim: The delay in posterior patterning is compensated by very rapid anterior shifts of posterior gap domains (especially gt) during the second half of the blastoderm stage in M. abdita.
source: This delay is compensated by very rapid anterior shifts of posterior gap domains (especially gt) during the second half of the blastoderm stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the steep slopes of boundary positions in Figure 3B during late time classes.

claim: Gap domains (the central Kr domain in particular) are wider in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Finally, gap domains (the central Kr domain in particular) are wider in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is shown by the distance between boundaries in Figure 3B.

claim: Wider gap domains lead to greater overlaps between adjacent expression domains in M. abdita.
source: This leads to greater overlaps between adjacent expression domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the wider domain widths observed in the data.

claim: The extended range of bcd in M. abdita is responsible for the more posterior initiation of gap gene expression.
source: The extended range of bcd in M. abdita is responsible for the more posterior initiation of gap gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from bcd expression data and its effects on gap gene positioning.

claim: The position of the posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain moves anteriorly as Bcd levels are reduced by RNAi in M. abdita.
source: The position of the posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain moves anteriorly as Bcd levels are reduced by RNAi.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 comparing wild-type to bcd RNAi embryos.

claim: The observed delay in posterior gap patterning in M. abdita could be linked to differences in cad expression.
source: The observed delay in posterior gap patterning could be linked to differences in cad expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of maternal cad in M. abdita and comparison with D. melanogaster.

claim: In D. melanogaster cad germ-line clones lacking maternal cad, posterior domains of gt are displaced towards the posterior.
source: Summary graphs comparing wild-type boundary positions (grey) to boundary positions in cad GLC (coloured lines) show posterior domains of gt (C) and abdominal domains of kni (F) that are displaced towards the posterior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with quantitative boundary data.

claim: In D. melanogaster cad germ-line clones lacking maternal cad, abdominal domains of kni are displaced towards the posterior.
source: Summary graphs comparing wild-type boundary positions (grey) to boundary positions in cad GLC (coloured lines) show posterior domains of gt (C) and abdominal domains of kni (F) that are displaced towards the posterior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F with quantitative boundary data.

claim: The resulting severe cuticle phenotypes from trunk gap gene RNAi in M. abdita are similar to those observed in the equivalent null mutants of D. melanogaster.
source: For the trunk gap genes, the resulting severe cuticle phenotypes are similar to those observed in the equivalent null mutants of D. melanogaster
evidence: This is based on comparison of observed RNAi phenotypes with published mutant phenotypes.

claim: There are two pairs of gap genes whose expression domains are mutually exclusive in D. melanogaster: hb and kni as well as Kr and gt.
source: In D. melanogaster, there are two pairs of gap genes whose expression domains are mutually exclusive: hb and kni as well as Kr and gt.
evidence: This is established knowledge about D. melanogaster gap gene expression.

claim: The same overall relative positioning of gap gene expression patterns is observed in M. abdita as in D. melanogaster.
source: We observe the same overall relative positioning of gap gene expression patterns in M. abdita (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown by the expression data in Figure 3.

claim: In M. abdita, mutually exclusive gap gene domains show a tendency to overlap slightly, especially during the early blastoderm stage.
source: However, in this species mutually exclusive domains do show a tendency to overlap slightly, especially during the early blastoderm stage, a phenomenon never observed in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is observed in the quantitative expression data comparing the two species.

claim: The complementary patterns of hb/kni and Kr/gt in D. melanogaster are established by strong mutual repression.
source: The complementary patterns observed in D. melanogaster are established by strong mutual repression between hb/kni and Kr/gt, respectively
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: In M. abdita hb knock-down embryos, the abdominal kni domain expands posteriorly.
source: In hb knock-down embryos (Figure 6A–C), the abdominal kni domain expands posteriorly (9/14)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita kni knock-down embryos, the anterior hb domain expands posteriorly.
source: In kni knock-down embryos (Figure 6D–F), the anterior hb domain expands posteriorly (35/52)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: Mutual repression between hb and kni is conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: In summary, our results indicate that mutual repression between hb and kni is conserved
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knock-down results showing reciprocal repression.

claim: The strength of repressive interactions between hb and kni differs considerably between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: but the strength of these repressive interactions differs considerably between M. abdita and D. melanogaster: we detect weaker inhibition of kni by hb and stronger inhibition of hb by kni.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the magnitude of boundary shifts in RNAi experiments between species.

claim: There is weaker inhibition of kni by hb in M. abdita compared to D. melanogaster.
source: we detect weaker inhibition of kni by hb and stronger inhibition of hb by kni.
evidence: This is inferred from the smaller expansion of kni in hb RNAi compared to D. melanogaster mutants.

claim: There is stronger inhibition of hb by kni in M. abdita compared to D. melanogaster.
source: we detect weaker inhibition of kni by hb and stronger inhibition of hb by kni.
evidence: This is inferred from the larger expansion of hb in kni RNAi compared to D. melanogaster mutants.

claim: In M. abdita Kr knock-down embryos, the anterior and posterior domains of gt expand into the central region of the embryo.
source: In Kr knock-down embryos (Figure 6G–I), we observe expansion of the anterior (17/20) and posterior (8/20) domains of gt into the central region of the embryo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: The cross-repressive interactions between Kr and gt are very similar in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: In addition, our results are consistent with the interpretation that the cross-repressive interactions between Kr and gt are very similar in both species
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects observed in RNAi/mutant experiments in both species.

claim: In M. abdita hb knock-down embryos, posterior gt fails to retract from the posterior pole.
source: In hb knock-down embryos (Figure 7A–C), posterior gt fails to retract from the posterior pole (24/35) or does not retract fully (4/35).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita gt knock-down embryos, the abdominal kni domain expands posteriorly.
source: In gt knock-down embryos (Figure 7D–F), the abdominal kni domain expands posteriorly (11/25).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita kni knock-down embryos, the central Kr domain shows a very pronounced expansion to the posterior.
source: In kni knock-down embryos (Figure 7G–I), the central Kr domain shows a very pronounced expansion to the posterior (26/40).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7I with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: The effect of Kr on hb is stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Accordingly, the effect of Kr on hb is stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the magnitude of hb boundary shifts in Kr RNAi/mutants between species.

claim: In M. abdita Kr knock-down embryos, the anterior hb domain expands posteriorly.
source: The anterior hb domain expands posteriorly in Kr knock-down embryos (21/41) (Figure 7J–L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7L with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita hb knock-down embryos, the central Kr domain expands towards the anterior.
source: In hb knock-down embryos, the central Kr domain expands towards the anterior (24/52; Figure 7Q,R).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7R with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: There is no evidence for anterior-to-posterior neighbour repression in M. abdita gap gene regulation.
source: In contrast, we do not find any evidence for anterior-to-posterior neighbour repression in M. abdita
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of clear effects in RNAi experiments that would indicate such repression.

claim: There is a strong asymmetry towards posterior-to-anterior neighbour repression in M. abdita.
source: In summary, our results indicate that there is a strong asymmetry towards posterior-to-anterior neighbour repression in M. abdita.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of effects observed across multiple RNAi experiments.

claim: Interactions involved in gap domain shifts are generally stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: The less ambiguous nature of the evidence compared to D. melanogaster suggests that interactions involved in gap domain shifts are generally stronger in this species.
evidence: This is inferred from the clearer and more pronounced effects observed in M. abdita RNAi experiments.

claim: The observed difference in the repressive balance between Kr and hb is essential to explain the altered dynamics of boundary positioning between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: The observed difference in the repressive balance between Kr and hb, in particular, is essential to explain the altered dynamics of boundary positioning between the two species
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between interaction strength differences and expression dynamics differences.

claim: In M. abdita tll knock-down embryos, the posterior hb domain is reduced in size.
source: In tll knock-down embryos, we find that the posterior hb domain is reduced in size (12/29) (Figure 8A2–3)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A3 with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita tll knock-down embryos, the anterior boundary of the posterior gt domain is displaced towards the posterior.
source: The anterior boundary of the posterior gt domain is displaced towards the posterior in some embryos (13/30), while it fails to retract completely (15/30) or does not retract fully (9/30) in others (Figure 8D2–3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D3 with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita hkb knock-down embryos, posterior hb is reduced in size.
source: In hkb knock-down embryos, we find that posterior hb is reduced in size (21/22) (Figure 8A4–5)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A5 with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita hkb knock-down embryos, the posterior gt domain is reduced in size and fails to retract.
source: The posterior gt domain is also reduced in size (8/10) and fails to retract (10/10) (Figure 8D4–5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D5 with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita tll hkb double knock-down embryos, posterior hb is strongly reduced in size.
source: In tll hkb RNAi embryos, we find that posterior hb is strongly reduced in size (15/15) (Figure 8A6–7)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A7 with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita tll hkb double knock-down embryos, the posterior gt domain is reduced and fails to retract.
source: The posterior gt domain is also reduced (21/36) and fails to retract (33/36) or does not retract fully (2/36) (Figure 8D6–7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D7 with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: In M. abdita tll hkb double knock-down embryos, abdominal kni shows posterior displacement.
source: Abdominal kni shows posterior displacement (16/16) (Figure 8C6–7)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C7 with quantitative boundary data from RNAi experiments.

claim: The regulatory effect of tll and hkb on trunk gap gene expression is similar in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that the regulatory effect of tll and hkb on trunk gap gene expression is similar in both species
evidence: This is inferred from comparing RNAi and mutant phenotypes between species.

claim: hkb may have a more prominent, and less redundant, role in regulating trunk gap genes in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: although hkb may have a more prominent, and less redundant, role in regulating trunk gap genes in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster, as indicated by the synergistic effect on Kr and kni expression observed in tll hkb double knock-downs.
evidence: This is inferred from the stronger effects observed in hkb single and tll hkb double knock-downs in M. abdita.

claim: Initial boundary positions are either more anterior or more posterior in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Initial boundary positions are either more anterior (dark grey) or more posterior (light grey background) in M. abdita (solid) than in D. melanogaster (dotted lines).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A comparing boundary positions between species.

claim: Boundary positions converge between M. abdita and D. melanogaster at different time points for different gap genes.
source: Arrows with time classes T1–T8 indicate when boundary positions first converge between the two species.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A with arrows indicating convergence times.

claim: Differences in expression dynamics between M. abdita and D. melanogaster are a consequence of the altered distribution of maternal co-ordinate gene products in M. abdita.
source: These differences in expression dynamics are a consequence of the altered distribution of maternal co-ordinate gene products in M. abdita.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between maternal gradient differences and gap gene expression differences.

claim: Posterior gap domains appear further posterior in M. abdita due to the broadened distribution and influence of bcd.
source: Posterior gap domains appear further posterior—due to the broadened distribution and influence of bcd
evidence: This is inferred from bcd expression data and its effects on gap gene positioning.

claim: Posterior gap domains shift to the anterior later in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster due to the absence of maternal cad.
source: and shift to the anterior later than in D. melanogaster—due to the absence of maternal cad.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of maternal cad in M. abdita and comparison with cad germ-line clones in D. melanogaster.

claim: The delayed posterior gap domain shifts in M. abdita are later compensated by pronounced, faster domain shifts in the second half of C14A.
source: This is later compensated by pronounced, faster domain shifts in the second half of C14A, an effect most clearly exhibited by Kr and gt
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A with steep boundary position changes during late time classes.

claim: The knock-down analysis of the gap gene network in M. abdita reveals a stronger posterior-to-anterior bias in cross-repression between neighbouring domains.
source: Correspondingly, our knock-down analysis of the gap gene network in M. abdita reveals a stronger posterior-to-anterior bias in cross-repression between neighbouring domains
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9C with thicker arrows indicating stronger interactions compared to Figure 9B.

claim: The more pronounced domain shifts of hb and posterior boundaries in M. abdita are caused by increased posterior cross-regulatory bias.
source: Taken together, this suggests that the more pronounced domain shifts of hb and posterior boundaries in M. abdita are caused by increased posterior cross-regulatory bias.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between interaction strength asymmetry and boundary shift dynamics.

claim: Different developmental dynamics and regulatory interaction strengths in the gap gene network produce extremely similar patterns at the onset of gastrulation in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Our analysis reveals how different developmental dynamics and regulatory interaction strengths in the gap gene network produce extremely similar patterns at the onset of gastrulation, despite significant differences in the initial phases of maternal co-ordinate and gap gene expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the convergence of expression patterns shown in the data.

claim: The observed phenomenon constitutes developmental system drift of a quantitative kind.
source: This constitutes developmental system drift of a quantitative kind: instead of changes in the qualitative nature of interactions (e.g., a switch from activation to repression), we observe neutral or compensatory evolution through tuning of regulatory interaction strengths.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that interaction types are conserved but strengths differ.

claim: Quantitative system drift in early embryonic patterning networks provides an explanation for the developmental hourglass model.
source: Finally, quantitative system drift in early embryonic patterning networks, as reported here for the cyclorrhaphan gap gene system, provides an explanation for the developmental hourglass model
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of divergence early and convergence later in development.

claim: The developmental hourglass model predicts a minimum of morphological divergence during intermediate embryonic stages.
source: This model predicts a minimum of morphological divergence during intermediate embryonic stages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the hourglass model.

claim: The developmental hourglass model has been confirmed at the level of gene expression in three recent studies.
source: It has been confirmed at the level of gene expression in three recent studies (Domazet-Lošo and Tautz, 2010; Kalinka et al., 2010; Quint et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Maternal co-ordinate and early gap gene expression differ significantly between M. abdita and D. melanogaster, but later converge to a common pattern.
source: We observe the same phenomenon in our explicitly spatio-temporal context: maternal co-ordinate and early gap gene expression differ significantly between species, but later converge to a common pattern
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A with divergent early patterns converging later.

claim: M. abdita fly culture and embryo collection/fixation were carried out as described in Rafiqi et al. 2011b and 2011c.
source: M. abdita fly culture and embryo collection/fixation were carried out as described in (Rafiqi, at al. 2011b; Rafiqi et al., 2011c).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used, citing previous protocols.

claim: Blastoderm stage embryos of M. abdita correspond to embryonic stages 4 and 5.
source: Blastoderm stage embryos of M. abdita—corresponding to embryonic stages 4 and 5 (Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1997; Wotton et al., 2014)
evidence: This is based on staging criteria from cited references.

claim: Blastoderm stage embryos were collected 4 hours after egg laying.
source: were collected 4 hr (hrs) after egg laying.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: RNAi treatment was carried out as described in Stauber et al. 2000, Lemke et al. 2008, and Rafiqi et al. 2011a.
source: RNAi treatment was carried out as described in Stauber et al. (2000); Lemke et al. (2008); Rafiqi et al. (2011a).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used, citing previous protocols.

claim: Two distinct dsRNA constructs were injected per gene in RNAi experiments, one being the knock-down agent, the other serving as a control.
source: Two distinct dsRNA constructs were injected per gene, one being the knock-down agent, the other one—with conserved domains excluded—serving as a control.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for RNAi experiments.

claim: M. abdita does not show any maternal cad expression.
source: Unlike D. melanogaster, M. abdita does not show any maternal cad expression (Stauber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation and confirmed by expression data in this study.

claim: Zygotic cad transcripts are first detected at C12 in M. abdita extending from around 34% A–P position to the posterior pole.
source: We first detect zygotic cad transcripts at C12 extending from around 34% A–P position to the posterior pole (Figure 10).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 with expression data.

claim: At C13, the anterior boundary of cad expression is at a similar position in M. abdita and D. melanogaster (31 vs 33% A–P position).
source: At C13, the anterior boundary of cad expression is at a similar position in M. abdita and D. melanogaster (31 vs 33% A–P position; Figure 10)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 comparing expression between species.

claim: cad retracts towards the posterior in D. melanogaster during C14A-T2 to T5.
source: However, at subsequent stages, cad retracts towards the posterior in D. melanogaster (39–42% A–P position during C14A-T2 to T5)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 with D. melanogaster expression data.

claim: cad maintains a stationary boundary at around 31–32% A–P position in M. abdita until around C14A-T5.
source: while it maintains a stationary boundary at around 31–32% A–P position in M. abdita (until around C14A-T5; Figure 10
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 with M. abdita expression data.

claim: tll expression is first detected at C12 in M. abdita in a domain at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position.
source: We first detect tll expression at C12 in a domain at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position (Figure 10).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 with expression data.

claim: The anterior tll domain in M. abdita does not appear until around C14-T4.
source: while the anterior tll domain in D. melanogaster appears in C13, its equivalent in M. abdita does not appear until around C14-T4 (Figure 10)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 comparing expression timing between species.

claim: hkb expression is first detected at C12 in M. abdita in two domains, one at the anterior pole extending to 8% A–P position, and one at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position.
source: We first detect hkb expression at C12 in two domains, one at the anterior pole extending to 8% A–P position, and one at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position (Figure 10).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 with expression data.

claim: Expression dynamics and boundary positions of hkb are very similar between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Other than that, expression dynamics and boundary positions are very similar to those reported for D. melanogaster (Figure 10)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 comparing expression between species.

claim: Maternal hb transcripts are uniformly distributed in M. abdita embryos.
source: Maternal hb transcripts are uniformly distributed in M. abdita embryos (Figure 11)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11 with expression data.

claim: A small posterior hb domain appears around C12 or C13 in M. abdita, extending to 90% A–P position.
source: Around C12 or C13, a small posterior hb domain appears in M. abdita, extending to 90% A–P position as in D. melanogaster (Figure 11)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11 with expression data.

claim: gt expression is first detected in M. abdita at C12 in an anterior stripe at 14–34% A–P position, and a posterior domain extending from 73% A–P position to the posterior pole.
